title: VLOOKUP & HLOOKUP
goal: Read and write VLOOKUP and HLOOKUP, avoid the column-number and TRUE traps, and know when to switch to XLOOKUP.

steps.text:
Open an old workbook and you'll often find **VLOOKUP**. It's the lookup everyone used before XLOOKUP arrived, and it still works in every version of Excel. Learn to **read** it.

`=VLOOKUP(F2,A2:D7,3,FALSE)` has four parts:
• `F2`: what to look for
• `A2:D7`: the whole table. The column you search must be its **first** column.
• `3`: which column of the table to bring back, counted from the left
• `FALSE`: exact match only

The **V** is for vertical (searches down a column). **HLOOKUP** is its sideways twin.

steps.prompt:
VLOOKUP wants the **whole table**, not just two columns. The first column (Code) is the one it searches.

Press on ==A2== and drag to ==D7==, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: Select the whole block of data, `A2` to `D7`: all four columns and all six rows. Leave out the headings.
clues: The Name Box shows `6R x 4C` when you have it right.

steps.prompt:
A customer wants the price of code **305** (==F2==). The Price is the **third** column of the table (Code, Item, Price).

In ==G2==, type `=VLOOKUP(F2,A2:D7,3,FALSE)`.
steps.explain: **320** is the price of the Saw. Excel found 305 in the first column, then went to the 3rd column of the same row. For the stock you'd write `4` instead.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use **VLOOKUP**: what to find, the table, the column number, FALSE.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Code 305 is the Saw, and the answer should be **320**. Count the columns from the left of the table: Code is 1, Item is 2, Price is 3.

steps.topic: Count from the table, not the sheet
steps.prompt:
Now the lookup column isn't column A. Staff IDs are in column **B**, so the table starts at ==B2==.

In ==G2==, find the **salary** of the ID in `F2`. Careful with the column number: you count from where the table starts.
steps.explain: **35000.** In the table `B2:D7`, ID is column **1**, Dept is **2**, Salary is **3**, even though Salary sits in sheet column D. Using 4 would give `#REF!`, because the table has only three columns.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The table is `B2:D7`, and you count its columns: ID = 1, Dept = 2, Salary = 3. A 4 gives `#REF!`, since there's no fourth column. Also end with `FALSE`.

clues: Column letters on the sheet don't matter. Count columns **inside** `B2:D7`.

steps.prompt:
Stock used to be the 4th column, and your formula was `=VLOOKUP(F2,A2:D7,4,FALSE)`. Then a colleague **inserted a Colour column** before Stock. Excel stretched your table to `A2:E7`, and the formula now reads as shown.

What does `G2` show for code 305?
options: Still the stock (6): Excel also fixes the 4
The colour (Black), with no error warning
steps.explain: Excel widens the table but never touches the **4**, so column 4 is now Colour. You get a confident wrong answer with no error. XLOOKUP points straight at the Stock column, so it follows it when columns move. That's the best reason to switch.
wrongFeedback: Excel updates ranges when you insert a column, but a typed number like 4 is just a number to it.
The table still has five columns, so 4 is still valid. No error.
clues: Which column is 4th in the new layout?

steps.prompt:
ID **1045** isn't on the staff list. In `F2`, someone wrote `=VLOOKUP(E2,A2:B6,2)`, **leaving off the last part**.

What do you think it shows?
steps.explain: Leave out the last part (or write `TRUE`) and VLOOKUP assumes your list is sorted and picks the **closest ID that isn't bigger**. That's 1040, Dev. Let's prove it.
wrongFeedback: That's what you'd **want**, but without FALSE VLOOKUP doesn't report a missing ID.
It steps down, never up. The closest ID that isn't bigger than 1045 is 1040.
clues: With no 4th part, VLOOKUP looks for the nearest smaller ID.

steps.prompt: Prove it. In ==F2==, type the formula exactly as it was, with no last part: `=VLOOKUP(E2,A2:B6,2)`.
steps.explain: **Dev.** No error, no warning, just the wrong person for an ID that doesn't exist. A real payroll file could pay the wrong person this way. **Always finish VLOOKUP with `FALSE`** (or `0`) unless you really want bands.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use **VLOOKUP** with three parts: the ID, the table, the column number.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Leave off the last part: `=VLOOKUP(E2,A2:B6,2)`. Excel will pick a name anyway.

steps.prompt:
Now fix it so the sheet tells the truth. In ==F2==, ask for an **exact** match, and if the ID isn't on the list, show "Not on list".

Wrap the lookup in **IFERROR**.
steps.explain: **Not on list.** `FALSE` stops the guessing, so a missing ID becomes `#N/A`, and `IFERROR` turns that error into words. Change `E2` to 1040 and you'd see Dev, correctly.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets, commas and quotes.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use both: **IFERROR** around **VLOOKUP**, with `FALSE` as the last part of the lookup.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The cell should say **Not on list**. Ask VLOOKUP for an exact match (`FALSE`), and give IFERROR the words in quotes.

steps.prompt:
This table runs **across**: months are in the top row. **HLOOKUP** searches the top row and brings back from the row number you give. Rows are counted **down from the top row of the table**, header included.

In ==B7==, find **Coffee's** sales for the month in `B6`. Coffee is the 3rd row of the table.
steps.explain: **210.** HLOOKUP found Mar across the top row, then went down 3 rows: header is 1, Tea 2, Coffee 3. Using 2 would give Tea's 150.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use **HLOOKUP**: month, table (headings row included), row number, FALSE.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Coffee in March is **210**. The table is `A1:E4`, and the row number counts the heading row as 1: header 1, Tea 2, Coffee 3.

clues: Same four parts as VLOOKUP, but the third is a **row** number.

steps.prompt:
A librarian knows a **title** (==D2==) and needs the **Book ID**. But the ID column is to the **left** of the titles, and VLOOKUP can only bring back columns to the right of the one it searches.

This is when you switch. In ==E2==, find the ID for the title.
steps.explain: **B104.** Search the titles, bring back the IDs on the left. XLOOKUP also defaults to an exact match and follows moved columns, which is why new files should use it.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: VLOOKUP can't look left. Use **XLOOKUP** here.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Search the **titles** (`B2:B7`) and bring back the **IDs** (`A2:A7`).

clues: XLOOKUP's three parts: what to find, where to look, what to bring back.

steps.prompt:
You inherit a five-year-old workbook full of working VLOOKUPs, and some colleagues still use Excel 2019, which has no XLOOKUP.

What's the sensible move?
options: Rewrite every VLOOKUP today, or the file will stop working
Leave the working ones alone; use XLOOKUP in new work you don't share with old Excel
Delete them: VLOOKUP no longer works
steps.explain: VLOOKUP works in every Excel version, so a working one isn't a problem. Use XLOOKUP for new formulas when everyone has Excel 2021 or 365. In Excel 2019, an XLOOKUP shows `#NAME?`.
wrongFeedback: Nothing forces a rewrite. A working VLOOKUP keeps working.
clues: Who opens the file? Do they have XLOOKUP?

steps.prompt:
The class teacher asks: **what did roll number 15 score?** The roll number is in ==F2==.

Put the marks in ==G2==.
steps.explain: **58** for Eshaan. Either lookup works here. XLOOKUP is shorter and has no column number to miscount.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Look the roll number up in the table.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Roll 15 is Eshaan, and the question asks for **marks**, the last column. With VLOOKUP, remember the exact-match `FALSE`.

clues: Search the Roll column, bring back Marks. Use whichever lookup you prefer.
